MOTION PICTURE AND BROADCASTING INDUSTRY FINAL-WAGE TIMING (LABOR CODE § 201.5) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Productions, Inc.

MOTION PICTURE / BROADCASTING INDUSTRY FINAL-WAGE TIMING — APPLICABILITY NOTE
California Labor Code section 201.5 sets a distinct final-wage timing rule for "an employee engaged in the production or broadcasting of motion pictures," as that statute itself defines the term — a different rule from the general immediate-on-discharge and 72-hour-on-quit deadlines in Labor Code sections 201 and 202 that apply to most other employees. This concerns Jordan Lee's employment with Acme Productions, Inc., recorded here as ending on October 1, 2026. Section 201.5's own timing rule and its own definitions, both described in the information that follows, turn on whether the work Jordan Lee performed for Acme Productions, Inc. falls within the statute's specific definition of covered work. Naming Jordan Lee and Acme Productions, Inc. here does not itself determine that Jordan Lee's job duties meet that statutory definition, and does not determine which final-wage timing rule applies to this particular employment relationship.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF WHO THIS SECTION COVERS
Labor Code section 201.5 defines "an employee engaged in the production or broadcasting of motion pictures," for purposes of that section's own timing rule, as an employee who meets two conditions at once: the employee's job duties relate to or support the production or broadcasting of motion pictures, or the facilities or equipment used in that production or broadcasting; and the employee is hired for a period of limited duration to render services relating to or supporting a particular motion picture production or broadcasting project, or is hired on the basis of one or more daily or weekly calls. The statute separately defines "daily or weekly call" as an employment that, by its own terms, will expire at the conclusion of one day or one week unless renewed. The statute also defines "production or broadcasting of motion pictures" broadly, covering the development, creation, presentation, or broadcasting of theatrical or televised motion pictures, television programs, commercial advertisements, music videos, or other moving images, made for entertainment, commercial, religious, or educational purposes, and presented by film, tape, live broadcast, cable, satellite transmission, webcast, or any other technology now in use or later adopted.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“An employee engaged in the production or broadcasting of motion pictures” means an employee to whom both of the following apply: (A) The employee’s job duties relate to or support the production or broadcasting of motion pictures or the facilities or equipment used in the production or broadcasting of motion pictures. (B) The employee is hired for a period of limited duration to render services relating to or supporting a particular motion picture production or broadcasting project, or is hired on the basis of one or more daily or weekly calls."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, motion picture/broadcasting employee definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.5.)
  "“Daily or weekly call” means an employment that, by its terms, will expire at the conclusion of one day or one week, unless renewed."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, "daily or weekly call" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.5.)
  "“Production or broadcasting of motion pictures” means the development, creation, presentation, or broadcasting of theatrical or televised motion pictures, television programs, commercial advertisements, music videos, or any other moving images, including, but not limited to, productions made for entertainment, commercial, religious, or educational purposes, whether these productions are presented by means of film, tape, live broadcast, cable, satellite transmission, Web cast, or any other technology that is now in use or may be adopted in the future."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, "production or broadcasting of motion pictures" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.5.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.5, subdivisions (a)(1), (a)(2), and (a)(4)), used as real evidence of how this specific section defines the category of employee and the category of industry activity it covers — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not itself a determination that any particular job duties or hiring arrangement meet this definition. The statute's definition has two conjunctive requirements (job duties tied to production/broadcasting, and limited-duration or call-based hiring); this clause does not resolve whether any specific role satisfies either requirement. The statute does not separately define a corresponding "motion picture industry employer" or "motion picture payroll services company" category within this section — this clause does not supply such a definition because the fetched text of Section 201.5 does not state one. The three citations below come from the same statutory subdivision, Section 201.5(a); they are treated as related definitional provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

THE CORE RULE: WAGES DUE BY THE NEXT REGULAR PAYDAY, NOT IMMEDIATELY
Labor Code section 201.5 states that a covered motion picture or broadcasting employee whose employment terminates is entitled to receive payment of wages earned and unpaid at the time of termination by the "next regular payday" — a distinct trigger from the general rule of immediate payment on discharge under Section 201 and the general 72-hour rule for an employee who quits without notice under Section 202. The statute defines "next regular payday," for purposes of this section, as the day designated by the employer, pursuant to Labor Code section 204, for payment of wages earned during the payroll period in which the termination occurs.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An employee engaged in the production or broadcasting of motion pictures whose employment terminates is entitled to receive payment of the wages earned and unpaid at the time of the termination by the next regular payday."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, motion picture/broadcasting final-wage due date (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.5.)
  "“Next regular payday” means the day designated by the employer, pursuant to Section 204, for payment of wages earned during the payroll period in which the termination occurs."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, "next regular payday" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.5.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.5, subdivisions (a)(3) and (b)), used as real evidence of this section's own final-wage due date and how the statute itself defines that due date — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination of what any particular employer's "regular payday" is or was for a given payroll period. Section 201.5's own definition of "next regular payday" cross-references Labor Code section 204, which sets the general rules for designating regular paydays; this clause does not independently quote or verify the text of Section 204 (it was reviewed only for context, not fetched and confirmed twice under this corpus's verification discipline), so this clause does not restate Section 204's own content and does not resolve how a specific payroll period's payday is determined. The two citations below come from the same statutory subdivisions, Section 201.5(a)(3) and (b); they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

MAILING OPTION AND THE STATUTE'S BROAD DEFINITION OF "TERMINATES"
Labor Code section 201.5 permits an employer to pay a covered employee's final wages either by mailing payment to the employee or by making it available at a location the employer specifies in the county where the employee was hired or performed labor; the statute deems payment made on the earlier of the date the wages are mailed or the date they are made available at that specified location. The statute also defines "terminates," for purposes of this section, broadly: an employment terminates when the employment relationship ends, whether by discharge, layoff, resignation, completion of employment for a specified term, or otherwise — meaning the next-regular-payday rule described elsewhere in this material is not limited to a discharge or a layoff, but also applies to a resignation or the natural expiration of a specified-term or call-based engagement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The payment of wages to employees covered by this section may be mailed to the employee or made available to the employee at a location specified by the employer in the county where the employee was hired or performed labor. The payment shall be deemed to have been made on the date that the employee’s wages are mailed to the employee or made available to the employee at the location specified by the employer, whichever is earlier."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, motion picture/broadcasting final-wage mailing option (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.5.)
  "For purposes of this section, an employment terminates when the employment relationship ends, whether by discharge, lay off, resignation, completion of employment for a specified term, or otherwise."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, "terminates" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.5.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.5, subdivisions (c) and (d)), used as real evidence of this section's own mailing option and its own definition of what counts as a covered termination — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular mailing or on-site availability in fact complies with the statute, or that any particular separation falls within the statute's definition of "terminates." This clause does not restate the substantive mechanics of the Section 203 waiting-time penalty (its accrual rate and 30-day cap), which this corpus addresses in its dedicated Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document rather than duplicating here. The two citations below come from the same statutory section, Section 201.5; they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

COLLECTIVE BARGAINING AGREEMENT CARVE-OUT
Labor Code section 201.5 states that nothing in the section prohibits the parties to a valid collective bargaining agreement from establishing alternative provisions for the final payment of wages to employees covered by this section, so long as those alternative provisions do not exceed the time limitation established in Labor Code section 204.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Nothing in this section prohibits the parties to a valid collective bargaining agreement from establishing alternative provisions for final payment of wages to employees covered by this section if those provisions do not exceed the time limitation established in Section 204."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, collective bargaining agreement carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.5.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.5, subdivision (e)), used as real evidence that this section's next-regular-payday rule can be varied by a valid collective bargaining agreement within a stated outer limit — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular collective bargaining agreement is valid, applicable to a given employee, or compliant with the Section 204 time limitation the statute references. This clause does not independently fetch or quote Section 204's own time limitation; it states only that Section 201.5 cross-references that limitation, an honest gap disclosed rather than resolved by assumption. This clause also does not determine whether any particular employee is covered by a collective bargaining agreement at all.

SECTION 203 WAITING-TIME PENALTY APPLIES TO A VIOLATION OF THIS SECTION
Labor Code section 201.5 does not state its own separate penalty for late payment. Instead, Labor Code section 203 expressly lists Section 201.5 among the final-wage statutes an employer's willful, unabated failure to comply with triggers the general waiting-time penalty: continuation of the employee's wages, as a penalty, from the due date at the same rate the employee was earning until paid or until an action is commenced, capped at 30 days, with an exception where the employee avoids or refuses tender of payment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, any wages of an employee who is discharged or who quits, the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced; but the wages shall not continue for more than 30 days."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 203(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, waiting-time penalty cross-reference (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=203.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 203, subdivision (a)), used as real evidence that Section 201.5 is one of the statutes listed as triggering the general Section 203 waiting-time penalty — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any particular late payment was "willful" within the meaning of Section 203, which is a separate legal standard this clause does not analyze here. This clause does not restate the full mechanics or the 30-day-cap arithmetic of the Section 203 penalty in detail, or its statute-of-limitations provision in subdivision (b); this corpus's dedicated Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document addresses those mechanics generally rather than this clause duplicating them. The single citation below is the operative text of Section 203(a) as currently in force; it is not corroborated by a second, independent source.
